query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic, single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, structural and chemical stability under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions is maintained at lower temperatures by high configurational entropy, but as the temperature increases toward the upper bound (~1923 K), atomic diffusion overcomes this stabilization and triggers elemental segregation and phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the operating temperature in a controlled catalytic (and thermoelectric) atmosphere from 473 K to 1923 K.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in situ (e.g., using high-resolution XRD/TEM with elemental mapping) under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions where thermal exposure and chemical reactivity are simultaneously present.
generation.structural_mediator: Activation of atomic diffusion that overcomes the kinetically hindering configurational entropy stabilization leads to elemental segregation and subsequent phase separation.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the high configurational entropy of the equiatomic, single-phase HEA suppresses phase separation. As temperature increases, the diffusion barriers become surmountable, permitting atomic rearrangements that result in the nucleation of secondary phases or elemental segregation, thereby compromising the original homogeneous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Below a certain temperature threshold, the HEA nanoparticles retain their single-phase solid solution structure; above this threshold, diffraction and elemental mapping data will reveal the emergence of secondary phases or compositional inhomogeneities due to activated diffusion.
generation.baseline: The baseline observation is the initial uniform, single-phase solid solution state as synthesized.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in systems without additional diffusion-barrier modifications (e.g., unmodified surfaces) and under uninterrupted catalytic/thermoelectric conditions; deviations may occur if extrinsic factors (e.g., protective surface treatments or non-reactive atmospheres) significantly alter diffusion kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold temperature at which diffusion activates sufficient elemental segregation is not precisely known and may depend on subtle variations in nanoparticle size, composition, and surface characteristics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles and subject them in a controlled catalytic/thermoelectric environment to a systematic step-wise increase in temperature from 473 K to 1923 K. Use in situ high-resolution TEM and XRD along with elemental mapping to observe structural and chemical evolution.
measurements: XRD patterns to detect changes in phase structure
TEM imaging for visualizing lattice reconstructions
Elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to assess elemental segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, despite surpassing the expected temperature threshold, the nanoparticles remain as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with no detectable signs of elemental segregation or secondary phase formation, the hypothesis that diffusion-activated segregation governs the stability breakdown will be falsified.

It is well known that the high configurational entropies may stabilize solid solutions in equiatomic, multi-element HEAs. Many attractive properties of HEAs are attributed to the effects induced by the structure of multi-element solid solution, such as large lattice distortion. F. Otto et al. [19] studied the microstructures of six equiatomic quinary alloys with analogous compositions and found that only one of the six alloys formed a single phase solid solution. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

frame.system: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution (i.e. high-entropy alloy nanoparticles).
frame.goal: Determine the mechanism that governs the maintenance of structural and chemical stability (i.e. resistance to phase separation, elemental segregation or lattice reconstruction) under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions across a wide temperature range (473–1923 K).
frame.limitation: It is not yet understood what fundamental factors or kinetic processes (such as configurational entropy contributions, diffusion barriers, or elemental segregation dynamics) control stability under these diverse operating environments.

prior_attempts: Previous studies on binary or ternary alloys have focused on phase stability at lower temperatures or under simpler chemical environments. These methods fell short in addressing the complex interplay of high configurational entropy, sluggish diffusion, and multi-component chemical interactions encountered in high-entropy nanoparticles over a broad temperature range.

decision.trend: Early HEA studies (e.g. PMC4999872) demonstrated that maintaining a single-phase solid solution can delay the nucleation of secondary precipitates under perturbative conditions (here ion irradiation) in multicomponent alloys, implying that high configurational entropy can stabilize structure until kinetic processes (such as diffusion‐induced segregation) become activated. Later work (e.g. PMC6908586) on HEAs exposed to aggressive high-temperature chemical environments revealed that even when a solid solution is initially formed, selective elemental dissolution and the formation of new precipitate phases can occur once the temperature is high enough to overcome intrinsic diffusion barriers. Overall, investigations have systematically moved from documenting the existence of delayed phase separation in bulk or thin-film HEAs to hinting at the dominant role of sluggish diffusion kinetics versus thermodynamic stabilization. However, none have yet fully addressed the competition between configurational entropy and kinetic accessibility in nanoparticles operating simultaneously under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions over a broad temperature range.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the balance between the large configurational entropy and the temperature‐dependent diffusion (or kinetic) barriers governs the onset of elemental segregation and phase transformation in equiatomic, single‐phase HEA nanoparticles under catalytic and thermoelectric environments. In particular, the quantitative temperature thresholds and operating conditions under which the slow diffusion becomes sufficiently activated to trigger phase separation or lattice reconstruction are not established.
decision.lever: Systematically vary operating temperature (across 473–1923 K) in a controlled catalytic atmosphere while using in situ high-resolution XRD/TEM with elemental mapping on nanoparticles with identical initial compositions. An additional lever could be to introduce subtle variations in surface treatments (or isotopic tracers) to modify diffusion barriers.
decision.why: This next step directly builds on the trend showing that HEA stability is maintained until kinetic processes (i.e. diffusion) overcome configurational entropy stabilization. By precisely controlling temperature and environment, the experiment can pinpoint the conditions under which diffusion‐mediated elemental segregation initiates, providing a testable mechanistic threshold that links the interplay of thermodynamics and kinetics to operational stability in nanoparticles.
